writing.rule: An absent or failed required check cannot be treated as a green release.
writing.explanation:
A reproducible release pipeline connects source checks to a specific revision. Formatting, compilation and tests answer different questions. A successful build does not establish that tests ran, and a test job from an older revision does not approve newer source.

The release policy requires fmt, test and build exactly once with successful results; extra unrelated checks may be present. Duplicate required records are ambiguous and should refuse delivery rather than choosing whichever result looks better. This lab models gate aggregation, while the companion workflow runs the actual commands in a clean checkout with Cargo.lock retained. The iOS terminal runs its supported Cargo profile; the desktop CI workflow exercises the server target, SQL migrations and integration requests. Keep those receipts separate instead of claiming one target qualifies the other.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run cargo fmt --check, cargo test and cargo build. Inspect the companion GitHub workflow for desktop integration checks.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

writing.task: Require exactly one successful result for each of fmt,test,build. Missing, failed or duplicate required results refuse release; unrelated checks do not affect this contract. Keep the public signature. Open the compiler lab and edit solution.rs; do not edit the private verification caller.
writing.success: The separate caller accepts the changed solution and rejects unchanged TODO, a wrong implementation and a printed success message.
writing.question: Does a successful build prove that the test job ran?
answers: Yes, building automatically runs every test
A missing check should default to success
No, it is a separate required observation
writing.feedback: Compilation success and independently executed tests provide different evidence.
